value.question: What does NASA mean by systems engineering, and what broad activities does the discipline cover?

steps.description: Search the NASA corpus for NASA's definition of systems engineering and the broad activities/phases the discipline covers (e.g., NASA Systems Engineering Handbook).
Find NASA's published systems engineering definition and activity scope to confirm and supplement the corpus findings.

key_findings: NASA defines systems engineering as "a methodical, multi-disciplinary approach for the design, realization, technical management, operations, and retirement of a system," and defines a system as the combination of elements that function together to produce the capability required to meet a need — including all hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, processes, and procedures (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p12-chunk-32).

The scope is life-cycle-wide and technical: technical planning addresses the scope of the technical effort, with the team identifying, defining, and developing plans for decomposition, definition, integration, verification, and validation of the system while orchestrating concurrent and cross-cutting engineering, distinct from program/project planning (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p126-chunk-485). Supporting activities named in the life-cycle material include defining the WBS, developing SOWs, acquiring SE tools and models, baselining a Systems Engineering Management Plan (SEMP), and allocating functions to hardware, software, and humans (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p34-chunk-120; nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p35-chunk-121).

SE is characterized as being about tradeoffs and compromises, using a broad crosscutting "big picture" view rather than a single-discipline view; the systems engineer is skilled in balancing organizational, cost, and technical interactions in complex systems and supports Project Planning and Control with accurate, timely cost and schedule information for technical activities (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p14-chunk-38).

The handbook presents a generic description of SE as it should be applied throughout NASA, aimed at increasing awareness and consistency across the Agency and advancing the practice of SE, and is intended as a companion for implementing NPR 7123.1, Systems Engineering Processes and Requirements, plus Center-specific handbooks and directives (nasa_Systems_handbook.pdf#p11-chunk-28).
gaps: No complete or authoritative enumeration of the broad activities the discipline covers: the evidence offers a definition, a technical-planning framing, and illustrative life-cycle tasks (WBS, SOWs, SEMP, functional allocation) rather than a bounded activity list or taxonomy.
The NPR 7123.1 process set that the handbook implements is not supplied, so the specific required SE processes and requirements cannot be stated or checked against the handbook's generic description.
The definitional passage is truncated in the evidence ("all things required to pr…"), leaving the full statement of what system elements and their interactions must produce unconfirmed.

Coverage of the later life-cycle phases (beyond Phase A) and detailed treatment of verification, validation, operations, and retirement activities is not evidenced, so how the discipline's activities change across the life cycle is unresolved.

The distinction between systems engineering and adjacent disciplines such as project management is only sketched through the technical-planning versus program/project-planning contrast; organizational placement, roles, and interfaces are not detailed.

value.text: NASA defines systems engineering as "a methodical, multi-disciplinary approach for the design, realization, technical management, operations, and retirement of a system," where a system combines all hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, processes, and procedures needed to meet a need. The discipline's activities span the life cycle: the technical team identifies, defines and plans decomposition, definition, integration, verification and validation, orchestrated with concurrent and cross-cutting engineering, distinct from program/project planning. Illustrative tasks include defining the WBS, developing SOWs, acquiring SE tools and models, baselining a Systems Engineering Management Plan, and allocating functions to hardware, software and humans. SE is about tradeoffs and compromises, taking a broad crosscutting "big picture" view rather than a single-discipline view and balancing organizational, cost and technical interactions. The handbook serves as a companion for implementing NPR 7123.1 across the Agency.

issues: The citation list omits the chunks that support several concrete claims (e.g., the WBS/SOW/SE-tools list and the SEMP baselining come from p34-chunk-120 and p35-chunk-121), so traceability is only partially documented.
The report drops the evidence's "Phase A" qualifier when mentioning baselining the Systems Engineering Management Plan, slightly generalizing the original statement.

value.answer: NASA defines systems engineering as "a methodical, multi-disciplinary approach for the design, realization, technical management, operations, and retirement of a system," where a system combines all hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, processes, and procedures needed to meet a need. The discipline's activities span the life cycle: the technical team identifies, defines and plans decomposition, definition, integration, verification and validation, orchestrated with concurrent and cross-cutting engineering, distinct from program/project planning. Illustrative tasks include defining the WBS, developing SOWs, acquiring SE tools and models, baselining a Systems Engineering Management Plan, and allocating functions to hardware, software and humans. key_points: NASA defines systems engineering as a methodical, multi-disciplinary approach covering a system's design, realization, technical management, operations, and retirement, where a system spans hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, processes, and procedures.

The scope is life-cycle-wide and technical: technical planning is distinct from program/project planning and covers decomposition, definition, integration, verification, and validation, orchestrated with concurrent and cross-cutting engineering.

Illustrative activities include defining the WBS, developing SOWs, acquiring SE tools and models, baselining a Systems Engineering Management Plan (SEMP), and allocating functions to hardware, software, and humans.

SE is characterized by tradeoffs and compromises, a broad crosscutting "big picture" view rather than a single-discipline view, and balancing organizational, cost, and technical interactions while supporting Project Planning and Control.

The handbook gives a generic agency-wide description of SE and is intended as a companion for implementing NPR 7123.1 and Center-specific handbooks and directives; the evidence does not supply NPR 7123.1's full process set or a bounded activity taxonomy.

citations.quote_or_summary: At NASA, "systems engineering" is defined as a methodical, multi-disciplinary approach for the design, realization, technical management, operations, and retirement of a system; a "system" includes all hardware, software, equipment, facilities, personnel, processes, and procedures needed to meet a need.

Technical planning addresses the scope of the technical effort; the technical team identifies, defines, and develops plans for performing decomposition, definition, integration, verification, and validation of the system while orchestrating concurrent and cross-cutting engineering.

Systems engineering is about tradeoffs and compromises; it uses a broad crosscutting view of the system rather than a single discipline view, and the systems engineer balances organizational, cost, and technical interactions in complex systems.
